extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students, critics, and practitioners of comedy (writers/comedians) researching dark/black comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for the genre of dark (black) humor: what counts as dark humor, how it functions, ethical/contextual considerations, and stylistic subtypes (e.g., grotesque vs ironic). Useful for creators and analysts of dark comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — subject matter and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor is a style of comedy that makes light of subject matter that is generally considered taboo, particularly subjects that are normally considered serious or painful to discuss, aiming to provoke discomfort, serious thought, and amusement for their audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the core defining criterion when evaluating or producing dark humor: target taboo/serious subjects and balance provoking discomfort, thought, and amusement. The article notes dark humor can occasionally relate to the grotesque genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from blue comedy and obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor differs from blue comedy — which focuses more on topics such as nudity, sex, and body fluids — and from obscenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or crafting material, separate 'dark' topical content (death, taboo suffering, existential themes) from purely sexual/obscene material (blue comedy); the aims and audience expectations differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to gallows humor (death-focused)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas the term dark humor is a relatively broad term covering humor relating to many serious subjects, gallows humor tends to be used more specifically in relation to death, or situations that are reminiscent of dying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If death or imminent death is the central subject, label/approach it as gallows humor; this narrower framing affects context and expected reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of the comedic stance — cynicism and skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Breton identified laughter in black humor as arising from cynicism and skepticism, often relying on topics such as death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful stylistic/tonal criterion: dark humor often arises from a skeptical or cynical stance toward subjects rather than naive lightness; this influences voice and rhetorical strategies (e.g., irony, bleak wit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of perspective — empathic victim vs mocking victim
rubrics_metrics.description: Breton's anthology included examples in which the wit arises from a victim with which the audience empathizes, as is more typical in gallows humor, and examples in which the comedy is used to mock the victim. In the last cases, the victim's suffering is trivialized, which leads to sympathizing with the victimizer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke aligns audience empathy with the victim (safer/therapeutic) or with the victimizer (ethical risk). Trivializing a victim's suffering is identified as an anti-pattern that can change moral alignment and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social functions — coping mechanism and morale effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Black comedy has the social effect of strengthening the morale of the oppressed and undermines the morale of the oppressors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider function as well as form: dark humor can be assessed by its social role (coping/solidarity vs punching-down). The article lists professions where it's common (police, firefighters, ambulance crews, military, journalists, lawyers, funeral directors) as contexts where it serves coping functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual appropriateness — insider vs outsider and teller identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul Lewis warns that this 'relieving' aspect of gallows jokes depends on the context of the joke: whether the joke is being told by the threatened person themselves or by someone else. Outsiders may not react the way those with mutual knowledge do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or judging dark humor, assess context: teller's relationship to the subject, audience composition, shared knowledge. Failure to account for context (telling an insider joke to outsiders) is an anti-pattern likely to offend or fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque satire vs ironic satire — technique and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque satire (satira grottesca) is contrasted with ironic satire; grotesque satire is described as working by 'addition' and often arouses a 'risata verde' (green laughter), producing laughter of despair and may 'make the horror of a story perceived.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish techniques: ironic satire may 'work by subtraction' while grotesque adds shocking elements to force perception of horror. Grotesque approaches can be more likely to cause pain or be judged out of taste; creators should weigh purpose (to reveal horror vs merely shock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical risk: trivialization and sympathizing with perpetrators
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the comedy is used to mock the victim, the victim's suffering is trivialized, which leads to sympathizing with the victimizer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative red flag: humor that trivializes suffering or reorients sympathy toward perpetrators is ethically problematic and risks harm or backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reception and psychological correlates
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2017 study concludes that people who appreciate dark humor 'may have higher IQs, show lower aggression, and resist negative feelings more effectively than people who turn up their noses at it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting reception, consider that appreciation of dark humor may correlate with particular cognitive/emotional traits; nevertheless, reception also heavily depends on context, identity, and cultural norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/literary precedents and genre expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary critics have associated black comedy and black humor with authors as early as the ancient Greeks (Aristophanes), and with writers such as Jonathan Swift, Rabelais, Vonnegut, Nabokov, etc.; the motive for the label is portraying profound or horrific events in a comic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators and evaluators can use historical examples to calibrate expectations and techniques; awareness of tradition (satire, Swiftian irony, grotesque) helps situate new work and set audience expectations.
